source: Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), "Farmer Notes" (ព្រឹត្តិប័ត្រ ព័ត៌មានកសិករ), Volume 26, Issue 4, April 2015 (បោះពុម្ពលើកទី ២៦ ឆ្នាំទី ១៦ លេខ ៣ ខែមេសា ឆ្នាំ២០១៥) — feature: "Watermelon variety 'Chan Amrit' (ពូជឪឡឹក ចន្ទអម្រឹត)", a CARDI-bred and released variety. A Publication of the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute.
text:
"Chan Amrit" is a watermelon variety bred and released by CARDI (Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute) following a variety improvement and selection program conducted over about three years (2003-2006).

Characteristics of Chan Amrit: the fruit matures around 60-65 days after sowing; the vine reaches flowering around 25-30 days and reaches harvestable maturity around 30-45 days after flowering; the fruit rind is medium-thick, roughly 3-4 mm; the fruit shape is oval/elongated, weighing roughly 8-10 kg on average; the fruit surface is smooth with light-green background and dark-green stripes, and the flesh is deep red with a sugar content (Brix) of about 8-9 (some figures given in the source are hard to read precisely due to scan quality and should be treated as approximate). The variety is noted as being well suited to Cambodian growing conditions and can be maintained by farmers as open-pollinated seed for replanting, since it is not a hybrid F1 variety.

Cultivation guidance for this variety: watermelon needs a growing area with good drainage, avoiding waterlogged and clay-heavy soils; land should be plowed to a fine tilth, and raised beds prepared with a bed width of about 4-4.5 m and furrow spacing worked out for the field. Two main planting methods are given: (1) direct sowing into the field, done by soaking seed in warm water for about 2 hours (roughly 40-90°C soaking water is referenced, treated cautiously as the exact reading is unclear) then sowing directly into prepared holes spaced across the bed at intervals of roughly 2 m by roughly 3 m, with about 3-4 seeds sown per hole and later thinned; germination is expected within about 7-9 days after sowing; and (2) transplanting nursery-raised seedlings, where seed is sown into nursery bags/trays and seedlings are hardened off in full sun for a few days before transplanting into the field at around 7-10 days old.

Plant spacing given is about 3 m between rows by 0.5-2 m within the row (row and in-row spacing figures vary somewhat between the source's text and diagram and should be cross-checked against the original before being treated as exact).

A fertilizer program table in the source lays out four top-dressing applications timed relative to transplanting/emergence: application 1 at about 7 days after transplanting; application 2 at about 14 days after transplanting, timed to just before flowering; application 3 timed at the start of fruit set; and application 4 timed at about 40 days after transplanting, when the fruit is enlarging. Fertilizer rates given per application are approximately 28-90 kg of urea, 60-90 kg of TE (triple superphosphate) blended with urea, and 60-90 kg of potassium sulfate, applied by broadcasting near the root zone and covering with soil, with a recommended overall program described as roughly balanced across urea, phosphorus, and potash split across the four applications (exact per-hectare totals in the source table are not fully legible from the scan and should be re-verified against the original CARDI bulletin before being used for precise dosing recommendations).

Harvest is expected around 60-65 days after sowing, and farmers are advised to check maturity signs (dried tendril near the stem, dull sound when tapped) similar to standard watermelon harvest practice, and to plan harvest timing around market demand, since overproduction in the same period in one area can depress farm-gate prices. The bulletin also notes it was published to share updated information with farmers, cooperatives, and other agricultural stakeholders, and lists CARDI's Kampong Speu-based Prateah Lang Research Station contact details for further advice.
